extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent agents/attorneys, and inventors preparing or prosecuting patent applications (primarily U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and definitional standards for drafting, prosecuting, and litigating patents under U.S. practice (MPEP-style glossary of legal requirements and quality criteria such as enablement, claim definiteness, duty of disclosure, novelty/obviousness standards, fees, and procedural steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that refers back to and further limits another claim (see: Claim, Dependent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to add narrower features; must properly depend from an earlier claim and is a drafting device to create claim hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the Invention (Specification Content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the specification that classifies the technical field, summarizes the technical background, and sets forth the features of the invention, with reference to drawings where included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must provide sufficient description to satisfy statutory requirements (see Application, Specification); include background, summary, detailed description and appropriate references to drawings and embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Patent Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect only the ornamental appearance or shape characteristics of an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents are numbered separately (preceded by D); drafting and claims must be limited to appearance/ornamentality (see MPEP 901.04, 1502).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure (Description & Enablement Requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure refers to an invention disclosure or portions of a patent application; it must be sufficient so one skilled in the art (1) understands what is being claimed (description requirement) and (2) can make and use the invention (enablement). In the U.S., the best mode must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure disclosures teach how to make/use the invention and particularly point out the claimed subject matter; reference MPEP 608, 2161, 2162 for detailed requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Support within a disclosure for a claimed invention such that a person skilled in the art is taught how to make and use the invention (MPEP 2164, 2164.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification to enable without undue experimentation; include detailed examples/embodiments where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling Disclosure (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A description sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers both 'how to make' and 'how to use' aspects; tie descriptions to claims to avoid insufficiency/invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of Disclosure / Inequitable Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An obligation on all persons involved in the patenting process to disclose information (patents, articles, lab data, etc.) to the Examiner that may affect patentability; failure can render a patent unenforceable (fraud on the PTO / inequitable conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and submit relevant prior art and material information (e.g., via IDS); sharing knowledge is required though a formal patentability search is not mandated. See MPEP 2001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Disclosure Statement (IDS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of patents, publications and other information submitted to the USPTO by an applicant to discharge the duty of disclosure or ensure consideration by the Examiner (MPEP 609).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File timely and complete IDS submissions to avoid later inequitable conduct issues; include relevant prior art citations and explanations where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S., the application must disclose the best mode of carrying out the invention (mentioned under Disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure specification describes the preferred embodiment and any known best mode to avoid invalidity under statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of Claim (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be sufficiently definite to provide a standard by which a third party can determine with some degree of certainty whether a practice would infringe; an indefinite claim fails to particularly point out the claimed invention (MPEP 706.03(d), 2171, 2173).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft clear claim language; avoid ambiguous terms and ensure claim scope can be reasonably ascertained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of the claim body that describe features of the invention and how those features interrelate (MPEP 608.01(m)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be structured so each essential element is identified and tied to the specification; missing essential elements can be grounds for rejection or invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-Plus-Function (Means for Claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim technique reciting an element as a 'means for' accomplishing a function (means-plus-function language), governed by MPEP 2181.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using means-plus-function language, the claim is interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification and equivalents; ensure specification discloses adequate structure to support such claims (avoid indefinite means-plus-function without disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Group Claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting members 'selected from the group consisting of …' which creates a limited form of generic claim; allowed only when members share at least one property primarily responsible for their function in the claimed relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure group members have a common property that justifies the Markush grouping to avoid rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment and Examples
rubrics_metrics.description: An embodiment is a concrete form of the invention described in the application; examples provide worked descriptions or alternative embodiments (MPEP 608.01(p), 2164.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative embodiments and worked examples to illustrate enablement and best mode; vary detail depending on complexity and predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Make and How to Use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'How to make' and 'how to use' are parts of the enablement obligation to ensure a person skilled in the art can practice the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient procedural steps, conditions, and parameters in the specification to enable manufacture and normal use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill / Hypothetical Person Skilled in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art is the baseline for judging enablement and obviousness; the relevant level depends on the nature of the technology and may include engineers, practitioners, or academics (MPEP 2141.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating enablement or obviousness, identify the appropriate skill level and ensure the disclosure and claims are drafted accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive Step / Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that an invention be not only new but also non-obvious to a person skilled in the art; the invention must not be merely an ordinary extension of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and argumentation to show non-obvious differences over the prior art; use secondary considerations (long-felt need, failure of others) where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Effective Date / Prior Art Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference's effective date determines whether it is prior art against a claimed invention; novelty requires the claimed invention not be fully anticipated by a prior art reference (Effective Date discussion and Local Novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish correct priority/filing dates (foreign, in-convention) and be mindful of prior publications and their effective dates when assessing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace Period and Experimental Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain jurisdictions (including limited U.S. rules) provide a grace period or allow experimental use such that public uses or disclosures within a specified pre-filing period may not bar a U.S. application; experimental use must be for testing/verification, not marketing (see MPEP 2133.03(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully document experimental testing vs public/commercial use; U.S. statutory bars typically apply one year after public disclosure or sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-File vs First-to-Invent
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems for awarding patent rights: 'First to file' awards the patent to the first filer (becoming global standard under TRIPs), while 'first to invent' awards to the first inventor (historically a U.S. principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File promptly to secure priority under first-to-file systems; preserve internal records and invention disclosures where first-to-invent rules may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Date and Foreign/Priority Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing date is when the application reaches the patent office in complete form; foreign filing dates (or in-convention filings within 12 months) can establish priority (see Paris Convention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure complete filings and claim priorities are timely; use foreign filing strategies to preserve priority rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information in the File History / File Wrapper Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The file history (file wrapper) contains all prosecution papers; narrowing amendments or representations made during prosecution can create prosecution history estoppel (file wrapper estoppel), limiting post-issue claim scope and application of the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in amendments and arguments during prosecution; avoid statements that later undermine claim scope or support an estoppel defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double Patenting and Terminal Disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting is the attempt to obtain more than one patent on the same invention or obvious variants; leads to double patenting rejections for improper multiple patents (see MPEP 804 series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address double patenting by distinguishing claims, filing terminal disclaimers when appropriate, or ensuring claims are patentably distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Claim Differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicial rule of claim construction that where two claims have apparently similar meaning, an effort should be made to interpret them so they have distinct meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claim sets with conscious differentiation between independent and dependent claims to reduce ambiguity and support broader/smaller scopes as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: An equitable doctrine that can find infringement even when accused product/process does not literally infringe, to prevent insubstantial changes that avoid literal infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that prosecution history estoppel and claim amendments can limit application; consider both literal and equivalent scope when drafting and enforcing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency / Insufficient Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A ground of invalidity where the description does not enable one skilled in the art to practice the invention (insufficient disclosure / failure to teach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid omitting essential elements, steps, or cooperative relationships in the specification and claims; include adequate detail and examples to support claimed subject matter (MPEP 608.01p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Evidence / Diligence (Reduction to Practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence is the activity required of an inventor (and attorney) prior to entry into another inventor's field and until reduction to practice or filing; for interference proceedings, diligence must be proven and corroborated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous records of experimentation, prototype fabrication, testing, ordering parts, and steps toward filing; corroborate where necessary (MPEP 2138.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference (Priority Determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority contest in the U.S. PTO to determine which of multiple parties was first to invent commonly claimed subject matter (MPEP 2300.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare documentary evidence of invention dates and diligence; note that interference practice is specific to U.S. pre-AIA rules and priority contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency / Inherent Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A property that is inherently present in something disclosed; inherent features can be treated as disclosed even if not explicitly stated, and may be described by amendment without introducing new matter (MPEP 2173.05(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inherent disclosure cautiously; when relying on inherent properties for novelty/obviousness or enablement, ensure the record supports the inherency finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: Limitation and Linking Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations are claim language that constrains breadth; linking claims join separate species or link product/process/apparatus claims (MPEP 809 series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claim sets to include proper limitations and linking claims where strategic; watch for restriction/election issues and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election/Restriction Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may be required to elect which distinct invention/claim to prosecute when multiple inventions are claimed; non-elected claims may be canceled without prejudice (see Restriction, MPEP 818, 809.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make careful election choices and consider refiling or pursuing divisional applications for non-elected inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Rejection / Applicant Options
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rejection is a claim rejection made final after the second or subsequent examination; applicant options include agreeing with Examiner suggestions, appealing, arguing prematurity, or amending claims (MPEP 706.07).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider interviews, appeal, amendments, or custodial arguments; one Examiner interview may be allowed where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees: Filing, Issue, Maintenance / Renewal / Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Various fees required during the patent lifecycle: filing fees at time of filing, issue fee prior to grant (timely paid within three months of allowance), maintenance (renewal) fees at statutory intervals (U.S.: 3.5, 7.5, 11.5 years), and petition fees for certain actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and timely pay required fees or face lapse; late fees/surcharges may permit limited reinstatement (see MPEP 1306, 2501, 2504, 509).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of Time (Office Action Responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions of the period for response to an Office Action may be available under specified rules (MPEP 710.02(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request extensions in accordance with PTO rules and pay any required extension fees; manage deadlines carefully to avoid abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: File History / Front Page / Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications include front pages listing bibliographic data and may include front-page drawings; drawings explain and describe the invention and are common for devices; chemical patents may use formulae and examples (MPEP 608.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear drawings where appropriate; include necessary figure legends in the specification (note: patent drawings do not have legends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Subject Matter Classes (Machine, Manufacture, Method, Composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter under U.S. law includes machines, manufactures, methods (processes), and compositions of matter (MPEP 2105 series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to clearly fall within a statutory class and describe embodiments corresponding to the claimed class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frivolous Invention / Utility Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that lacks utility (serves no purpose or use) is a frivolous invention and not patentable (MPEP 706.03(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate a specific, substantial, and credible utility in the specification to meet the utility requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening Rights (Reissue / Reexamination Effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense arising when a patent is later reissued with broader claims due to error; persons who practiced the broadened claims prior to reissue may have intervening rights to continue practice without infringement (MPEP 1460).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider intervening rights implications when amending or reissuing patents; drafting and prosecution strategies can affect third-party rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity Grounds (Novelty, Obviousness, Insufficiency, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can be invalidated if it fails statutory requirements such as novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), enablement/insufficiency, or definiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and address potential invalidity grounds in drafting and prosecution; use comprehensive prior art searches and well-supported disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud on the Patent Office / Inequitable Conduct Sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional withholding or misrepresentation of material information before the PTO can constitute fraud/inequitable conduct and render a patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain truthful communications, timely disclose material references, and document decision-making about what to disclose; avoid any conduct that could be characterized as deceitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement Standards: Literal and By Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement occurs when an accused product/process contains every recital of a claim; infringement by equivalents applies when differences perform identical functions in substantially the same way to achieve the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting and evaluating patents, consider both literal claim scope and potential doctrine of equivalents coverage; prosecution history estoppel can limit equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages: Lost Profits vs Reasonable Royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits measure damages tied to profits the patentee would have earned but for infringement; when lost profits are not provable, damages are measured by a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve records and economic evidence to support lost profits claims where possible; licensing and market data are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Family / Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that relate to the same invention and share the same priority application form a patent family; equivalents together may form family coverage across jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate international filings to build a family; track corresponding foreign documents and publication kinds (INPADOC, ECLA, IPC classifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and Search Resources (IPC, ECLA, Derwent, Dialog, Lexis-Nexis, Micropatent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of international and national classification systems (IPC, ECLA, US classification) and commercial databases (Derwent, Dialog, Lexis-Nexis, Micropatent) to conduct patent searches and competitive intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate classification schemes and databases for thorough prior art searching; combine sources for best coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission Options: Disclosure Document Program / H Document / Statutory Invention Registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs exist (Disclosure Document Program, H document/SIR) that provide limited evidentiary benefits or publication without patent grant (e.g., SIR to prevent others from patenting), but do not create patent protection (MPEP 1706).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand limitations of such programs; prefer full patent filings for protection, and use confidential disclosures with independent witnesses for corroboration where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace Period / Local Novelty Differences Across Jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace period doctrines and local novelty rules vary by country (e.g., local novelty may limit invalidation to publications in the granting country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan international disclosure and filing strategies to account for jurisdictional differences; timely foreign filings can preserve priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescription for Claims Drafting to Avoid File-Wrapper Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowing amendments and representations during prosecution can preclude asserting broader interpretations after issuance (file wrapper/prosecution history estoppel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and make prosecution remarks judiciously; consider alternatives such as continuations to preserve broader claim possibilities.
